name: Layers of Guard
description: Understand how feet, knees, and arm frames protect your guard at different distances, then practice replacing a lost barrier before the passer controls your torso.
summary: Think of guard layers as the barriers still separating a passer from your torso: feet and shins, knees, and arm frames.
overview: When a foot gets cleared, look for what still works before trying to rebuild everything. These barriers overlap and change with the guard; there is no universal order that every pass must follow.
key_takeaways: At longer range, feet and shins can manage distance while your hips stay facing the passer.
As distance closes, a knee or shin between the bodies may preserve room to move your hips.
Arm frames can buy space for leg recovery, but reaching with both arms can leave your torso exposed.
Keep one useful barrier while replacing another. Reaching for a distant foot placement may sacrifice the frame you already have.
An underhook is a positional choice, not a final layer that makes every guard safe.

bjj_applications.scenario: A standing passer knocks one foot off their hip
bjj_applications.application: Use the other leg and a suitable hand connection to manage distance as you turn to face them. Replace the cleared foot when there is room.
bjj_applications.outcome: You repair one missing barrier without giving up the remaining one.

bjj_applications.scenario: Your half guard knee shield is being folded down
bjj_applications.application: Keep your arms inside and prevent the passer from freely controlling your head. Make space to rebuild the shield or another guard connection.
bjj_applications.outcome: You have something to work behind even if the original shield cannot be restored.

bjj_applications.scenario: The passer reaches your hip while your legs trail behind
bjj_applications.application: Use a frame to keep their torso from settling onto yours, then move your hips to bring a knee back inside. If they settle the pin, switch to an escape rather than reaching for their far hip with your foot.
bjj_applications.outcome: You distinguish an available guard recovery from an established pin that needs different work.

common_mistakes.mistake: Trying to put the feet back first at every distance
common_mistakes.consequence: The leg may have no path inside, and the reach opens the space beside your ribs.
common_mistakes.correction: Use the nearest workable frame or knee to make room before extending a leg.

common_mistakes.mistake: Counting barriers instead of checking their function
common_mistakes.consequence: A foot touching the passer does little if it cannot affect distance or follow their movement.
common_mistakes.correction: Ask what the contact stops and whether your hips can still face the passer.

training_exercises.name: Replace one barrier
training_exercises.description: Start in open guard with feet or shins making contact. Top clears one contact at a time while bottom follows and replaces it. Begin slowly, then add resistance; reset when top reaches a settled torso pin or bottom re-establishes both leg contacts.
training_exercises.focus: Keep a useful connection during the repair.

training_exercises.name: Close-range recovery
training_exercises.description: Start with the passer beside the knees and bottom holding an arm frame, without a settled pin. Bottom tries to bring a knee inside; top tries to close the space. Reset on either result and switch sides.
training_exercises.focus: Use the remaining barrier to recover a stronger one.

knowledge_assessment.question: Must a passer clear feet, knees, arms, and an underhook in that order?
knowledge_assessment.answer: No. Those contacts overlap, and passes can bypass some of them. Look at what blocks the passer in the actual position.

knowledge_assessment.question: How does this differ from the phases of guard?
knowledge_assessment.answer: Layers describe the physical barriers you have. Phases describe whether your immediate priority is engagement, attack, or recovery.
